summary: A 1977 Telnet option that lets a user log out cleanly, so one side can ask the other to end the session. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: This gives people a polite way to say goodbye and close a remote session properly instead of just disconnecting.

subtitle: A Telnet option that lets one side forcibly log out the other side's user process instead of leaving it detached.

tldr.problem: Closing a connection to a hung host often only detaches the user process, which can keep loading the system, and a normal logout can take a long time.
tldr.mechanism: The LOGOUT option (code 18) lets one side send IAC DO LOGOUT, and the receiver agrees with IAC WILL LOGOUT and forcibly logs off the user process at its end.
tldr.outcome: A user can abandon a hung session cleanly, and a server can use the same option to warn of an impending auto-logout.

today: RFC 727 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata records no RFC obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why a Forced Logout
sections.content:
A runaway user process can hang so it cannot be interrupted, or the system can be so bottlenecked that delays are intolerable. The user eventually closes the connection, but many hosts merely detach the process so an accidental close does not lose the job, and the user can attach again later. If the user is giving up completely, that hung job continues to load the system.

The option lets a process instruct the server that the user process should be forcibly logged out instead of detached. A secondary use is for a server to warn of impending auto-logout due to inactivity.
sections.eli5: Closing the door does not always turn off the lights. This lets you say 'turn everything off for real'.

sections.title: The Four Commands
sections.content:
The option is named LOGOUT and has code 18. IAC WILL LOGOUT requests permission to, or confirms it will, forcibly log off the user process at the sender's end. IAC WON'T LOGOUT refuses to. IAC DO LOGOUT requests that the receiver do so, or confirms permission. IAC DON'T LOGOUT demands that the receiver not forcibly log off.

The default is WON'T LOGOUT and DON'T LOGOUT: no forcible logging off of the server's user process.
sections.eli5: There are four little phrases: 'I will log out', 'I won't', 'please log out', and 'please don't'.

sections.title: How It Works
sections.content:
When a user wants to leave and not wait for the host's normal logout, it sends IAC DO LOGOUT. The receiver may answer IAC WILL LOGOUT and then forcibly log off the user process. If it answers IAC WON'T LOGOUT, the process very possibly will be detached if the connection breaks.

An impatient user could send IAC DO LOGOUT and then close. At worst the server ignores it and detaches. A server implementing the option should log out despite the sudden close, and it starts the logout immediately without waiting for the user to receive the confirmation.
sections.eli5: You say 'please log me out' and the computer starts right away, even if you have already walked out of the room.

sections.title: Auto-Logout Warning
sections.content:
In the RFC's second case, a user is idle long enough to approach the server's autologout time. Shortly before it, the server sends IAC WILL LOGOUT. The user sees this and sends IAC DON'T LOGOUT and continues working.

Nothing stops the server from logging out the process if inactivity continues. This prevents a malicious user from locking up a process by answering every IAC WILL LOGOUT with IAC DON'T LOGOUT and doing nothing else.
sections.eli5: The computer says 'you have been quiet, I may log you out'. If you wave back, you get more time, but not forever.
